questions.question: Cultural values can influence how people think about sexuality.
questions.memo: Cultural values are among the influences that shape views on sexuality.

questions.question: Pressure from friends to act a certain way is ____ pressure.
questions.memo: Peer pressure can influence decisions about relationships and behaviour.

questions.question: Problem-solving skills help with identity and sexuality by…
options: helping you think through choices calmly
questions.expected: helping you think through choices calmly
questions.memo: Problem-solving skills help you weigh options and make calm, informed choices.

questions.question: It is healthy to respect that people develop and feel things at different paces.
questions.memo: People mature and feel things at different paces; respecting this is healthy.

questions.question: Which is the most reliable source of information about your development?
options: A nurse, doctor, teacher or parent
questions.expected: A nurse, doctor, teacher or parent
questions.memo: Health professionals and trusted adults give reliable information.

questions.question: Sort each into a HEALTHY or UNHEALTHY way to handle questions about growing up.

items.text: Ask a trusted adult or health worker
Feel ashamed and ask no one

questions.expected: Asking trusted adults and using reliable info are healthy; believing rumours or hiding in shame are not.
questions.memo: Reliable information and trusted adults are healthy; rumours and shame are not.

questions.question: Understanding influences on your choices helps you make your own healthy decisions.
questions.memo: Recognising what influences you helps you make independent, healthy decisions.

questions.question: The healthiest overall attitude to sexuality at this age is to…
options: understand it as natural and make informed, value-based choices
questions.expected: understand it as natural and make informed, value-based choices
questions.memo: Seeing sexuality as natural and making informed, value-based choices is healthiest.

questions.question: Different people develop and feel things at different paces, and that is normal.
questions.memo: Everyone matures at their own pace; respecting this is part of healthy development.

LO.G8.DS.A3.title: Relationships and friendships
LO.G8.DS.A3.description: Development of the self in society (CAPS G8 T1) — Development of the self in society: Relationships and friendships.
LO.G8.DS.A3.strand: Development of the self in society · Term 1
LO.G8.DS.A3.caps_topic: Development of the self in society
LO.G8.DS.A3.recovery_strategy: Healthy relationships are built on respect, good communication and honesty.

questions.question: What is the basis of a HEALTHY relationship?
questions.memo: Healthy relationships are built on respect, trust, honesty and communication.

questions.question: Relationships happen at home, at school and in the community.
questions.memo: We have relationships in many settings — home, school and community.

questions.question: Which is an APPROPRIATE way to start a friendship?
options: Be friendly, show interest and find common ground
questions.expected: Be friendly, show interest and find common ground
questions.memo: Genuine friendliness and shared interests are healthy ways to start a friendship.

questions.question: Keeping a friendship going over time is called ____ a relationship.
questions.memo: Sustaining a relationship means keeping it healthy and strong over time.

questions.question: How can you SUSTAIN a healthy friendship?
options: Communicate, support each other and resolve conflict respectfully
Compete and put each other down
questions.expected: Communicate, support each other and resolve conflict respectfully
questions.memo: Communication, support and respectful conflict resolution sustain friendships.

questions.question: Being able to disagree in a constructive way is a useful communication skill.
questions.memo: Constructive disagreement keeps relationships honest and respectful.

questions.question: Which sign suggests a friendship is UNHEALTHY?
options: One person controls or constantly criticises the other
questions.expected: One person controls or constantly criticises the other
questions.memo: Control, constant criticism or disrespect are signs of an unhealthy relationship.

questions.question: Ending a relationship kindly and respectfully shows ____.
questions.memo: Ending a relationship respectfully, without cruelty, shows maturity.

questions.question: It is sometimes healthy to end a relationship that is harmful.
questions.memo: Ending a harmful relationship, done respectfully, can be a healthy choice.

questions.question: Two friends disagree about plans. The healthiest approach is to…
options: talk it out and find a fair compromise
give each other the silent treatment
questions.expected: talk it out and find a fair compromise
questions.memo: Talking openly and compromising resolves conflict and protects the friendship.

questions.question: Which is an example of GOOD communication in a relationship?
options: Listening and saying how you feel honestly
questions.expected: Listening and saying how you feel honestly
questions.memo: Listening and honest expression are signs of good communication.

questions.question: Trust, once broken, can sometimes be rebuilt with honesty and time.
questions.memo: With honesty, effort and time, broken trust can sometimes be rebuilt.

questions.question: Treating a friend the way you would like to be treated shows mutual ____.
questions.memo: Mutual respect — treating each other well — is central to healthy relationships.

questions.question: A friend pressures you to drop another friend 'or else.' This is a sign of…
questions.memo: Ultimatums and control are signs of an unhealthy, controlling friendship.

questions.question: Healthy friendships allow each person to have other friends and interests.
questions.memo: Healthy friendships are not possessive; each person keeps their own friends and interests.

questions.question: Appropriate behaviour in a relationship includes…
questions.memo: Honesty, kindness and respecting boundaries are appropriate relationship behaviours.

questions.question: Sort each behaviour into HEALTHY or UNHEALTHY in a friendship.

items.text: Listening when there is a problem
Controlling who the other can see

questions.expected: Support and listening are healthy; controlling and insulting are unhealthy.
questions.memo: Healthy relationships support and respect; unhealthy ones control and demean.

questions.question: Put the steps for resolving a disagreement with a friend in order.
questions.expected: Calm down, listen to both sides, find a fair compromise, then agree and move on.
questions.memo: Resolve conflict by calming down, listening, compromising and moving on respectfully.

questions.question: The deeper purpose of learning relationship skills is to…
options: build healthy, respectful connections throughout life
questions.expected: build healthy, respectful connections throughout life
questions.memo: Relationship skills help you build healthy, respectful connections for life.

questions.question: In a healthy friendship, both people feel respected and free to be themselves.
questions.memo: Mutual respect and freedom to be yourself are signs of a healthy friendship.

LO.G8.HE.A1.title: Social factors in substance abuse
LO.G8.HE.A1.description: Health, social & environmental responsibility (CAPS G8 T2) — Health, social and environmental responsibility: Social factors in substance abuse.
LO.G8.HE.A1.recovery_strategy: Friends, community and media can push substance use; refusal skills help you resist.

questions.question: Which is a SOCIAL factor that can contribute to substance abuse?
questions.memo: Social factors include community norms and media that can encourage substance use.

questions.question: Media can sometimes make alcohol or drug use look attractive.
questions.memo: Media images can glamorise substances, influencing young people.

questions.question: What is a 'refusal skill'?
options: The ability to say no clearly and confidently
A way to give in politely
questions.expected: The ability to say no clearly and confidently
questions.memo: Refusal skills let you say no to substances clearly and confidently.

questions.question: Saying 'No thanks, I don't do that' in a firm, calm way is a ____ skill.
questions.memo: A firm, calm 'no' is a refusal skill that helps resist pressure.

questions.question: Which is a SHORT-TERM consequence of substance abuse?
questions.memo: Short-term consequences include poor judgement, accidents and risky behaviour.

questions.question: Which is a LONG-TERM consequence of substance abuse?
questions.memo: Long-term consequences include addiction, health damage and harm to relationships.

questions.question: Substance abuse can be linked to crime and violence.
questions.memo: Substance abuse is linked to crime, violence and poor educational outcomes.

questions.question: Treatment programmes that help people recover from addiction provide ____.
questions.memo: Rehabilitation helps people recover from substance dependence.

questions.question: Where can someone find help, care and support for a substance problem?
questions.memo: Clinics, counsellors and SANCA offer help, care and support.

questions.question: Saying no to substances is a sign of weakness.
questions.memo: Refusing substances shows strength and good decision-making, not weakness.

questions.question: At a party, friends pressure Sipho to drink. The BEST refusal is to…
options: calmly say no and suggest something else to do
questions.expected: calmly say no and suggest something else to do
questions.memo: A calm, firm refusal with an alternative resists pressure while keeping the peace.

questions.question: How does the community influence substance abuse?
options: Easy access and acceptance can increase use
questions.expected: Easy access and acceptance can increase use
questions.memo: Community factors like easy access and acceptance can increase substance use.

questions.question: Decision-making skills help a person avoid substance abuse.
questions.memo: Good decision-making helps people weigh consequences and avoid substance abuse.

questions.question: Substance abuse can lead to poor results and dropping out of ____.
questions.memo: Substance abuse is linked to poor educational outcomes and dropping out.

questions.question: Why is it important to know where to find help?
options: So you or a friend can get support early
questions.expected: So you or a friend can get support early
questions.memo: Knowing where to find help means support can come early, before harm worsens.

questions.question: Supporting a friend to get help is a caring, responsible action.
questions.memo: Helping a friend reach support is caring and responsible.

questions.question: Sort each consequence of substance abuse into SHORT-TERM or LONG-TERM.
questions.expected: Poor judgement and accidents are short-term; addiction and health damage are long-term.
questions.memo: Some harms appear immediately; others build up over the long term.

questions.question: Put the steps of a good refusal in a tricky situation in order.

items.text: Recognise the pressure and the risk
Suggest an alternative or excuse to leave

questions.expected: Recognise the risk, refuse clearly, offer an alternative, then leave the situation.
questions.memo: Refuse well by recognising the risk, saying no, offering an alternative and leaving.

questions.question: The best way to avoid substance abuse is to…
options: build strong refusal skills and positive support
questions.expected: build strong refusal skills and positive support
questions.memo: Refusal skills and positive support are the best protection against substance abuse.

questions.question: Helping a friend reach support for a substance problem is a caring, responsible act.
questions.memo: Supporting a friend to get help is caring and responsible, not a betrayal.

LO.G8.HE.A2.title: Environmental health issues
LO.G8.HE.A2.description: Health, social & environmental responsibility (CAPS G8 T2) — Health, social and environmental responsibility: Environmental health issues.
LO.G8.HE.A2.recovery_strategy: Laws and small everyday actions both help protect the environment and our health.

questions.question: Why do governments make LAWS to protect environmental health?
options: To stop pollution and protect people and nature
questions.expected: To stop pollution and protect people and nature
questions.memo: Environmental laws aim to reduce pollution and protect people and the environment.

questions.question: Following environmental laws is part of being a responsible citizen.
questions.memo: Obeying environmental laws and policies is part of responsible citizenship.

questions.question: What is 'Earth Day' about?
options: Caring for and protecting the planet
questions.expected: Caring for and protecting the planet
questions.memo: Earth Day raises awareness about protecting and preserving the environment.

questions.question: A set of planned actions to improve the environment is an environmental health ____.
questions.memo: An environmental health programme is a planned set of actions to improve the environment.

questions.question: Which is a way of 'being kinder to Earth'?
questions.memo: Reduce, reuse, recycle and conserving resources are ways to be kinder to Earth.

questions.question: Laws and policies can be used to address an environmental issue.
questions.memo: Applying laws and policies is one way to address environmental issues.

questions.question: Air pollution is mainly harmful because it…
questions.memo: Air pollution harms human health and the environment.

questions.question: Protecting nature so future generations can enjoy it is called ____ of the environment.
questions.memo: Preservation means protecting the environment for the future.

questions.question: A school wants to run an environmental health programme. A good first action is to…
options: identify a local environmental problem to target
questions.expected: identify a local environmental problem to target
questions.memo: A good programme starts by identifying a specific local environmental problem.

questions.question: Individuals can support environmental laws through their daily choices.
questions.memo: Everyday choices, like recycling and saving water, support environmental protection.

questions.question: Which everyday action best reduces waste?
questions.memo: Reusing and recycling reduce waste sent to landfill.

questions.question: Why involve the whole community in an environmental programme?
options: Shared effort makes a bigger, lasting difference
questions.expected: Shared effort makes a bigger, lasting difference
questions.memo: Community involvement makes environmental programmes more effective and lasting.

questions.question: Saving electricity reduces pollution from power stations.
questions.memo: Using less electricity reduces the pollution created in generating it.

questions.question: Cutting down too many trees, or ____, harms the environment.
questions.memo: Deforestation — clearing too many trees — damages ecosystems and the climate.

questions.question: How does honouring Earth Day help year-round?
options: It reminds people to keep good environmental habits
questions.expected: It reminds people to keep good environmental habits
questions.memo: Earth Day reminds people to keep environmentally friendly habits all year.

questions.question: Environmental health and human health are closely connected.
questions.memo: A healthy environment supports human health; pollution harms both.

questions.question: Sort each action into PROTECTS the environment or DAMAGES it.
questions.expected: Recycling and saving water protect; dumping and polluting damage the environment.
questions.memo: Conserving and recycling protect the environment; dumping and pollution damage it.

questions.question: Put the steps for running an environmental health programme in order.
questions.expected: Identify the issue, plan actions, carry them out, then review and improve.
questions.memo: An environmental programme: identify, plan, act, then review.

questions.question: The main message of environmental responsibility is that…
options: everyone shares the duty to protect the environment
questions.expected: everyone shares the duty to protect the environment
questions.memo: Protecting the environment is a shared responsibility for everyone.

questions.question: Small daily habits, like recycling, add up to a big environmental difference.
questions.memo: Everyday habits across many people add up to a large positive environmental impact.

LO.G8.HE.A3.title: Decisions about HIV and AIDS
LO.G8.HE.A3.description: Health, social & environmental responsibility (CAPS G8 T2) — Health, social and environmental responsibility: Decisions about HIV and AIDS.
LO.G8.HE.A3.recovery_strategy: HIV can be managed with medication and healthy living; prevention and care reduce its spread and stigma.

questions.question: What does HIV stand for in simple terms?
options: A virus that weakens the body's immune system
questions.expected: A virus that weakens the body's immune system
questions.memo: HIV is a virus that attacks the immune system; with treatment it can be managed.

questions.question: With medication and healthy living, a person with HIV can live a long life.
questions.memo: Treatment, a good diet and healthy living let people with HIV live long, healthy lives.

questions.question: Which helps MANAGE HIV?
options: Taking medication as prescribed and eating well
questions.expected: Taking medication as prescribed and eating well
questions.memo: Managing HIV means taking medication correctly, eating well and living healthily.

questions.question: Medication that helps control HIV is called ____ treatment (ARVs).
questions.memo: Antiretroviral (ARV) treatment helps control HIV and keeps people healthy.

questions.question: Which is a way to PREVENT the spread of HIV?
questions.memo: Prevention includes abstinence and safe, informed, responsible choices.

questions.question: You can tell who has HIV just by looking at them.
questions.memo: You cannot tell who has HIV by appearance; assuming so causes unfair stigma.

questions.question: How should we treat people living with HIV and AIDS?
options: With care, respect and no discrimination
questions.expected: With care, respect and no discrimination
questions.memo: People with HIV deserve care, respect and freedom from discrimination.

questions.question: Unfair judgement of people with HIV is called ____.
questions.memo: Stigma is unfair judgement; it harms people and discourages testing and treatment.

questions.question: Caring for someone with HIV includes emotional support, not just medicine.
questions.memo: Care includes emotional support and respect, alongside medical treatment.

questions.question: A classmate is known to be HIV positive. The responsible, kind attitude is to…
options: treat them as a normal friend and support them
questions.expected: treat them as a normal friend and support them
questions.memo: Treating them normally and offering support is responsible and kind; HIV is not spread by everyday contact.

questions.question: Responsible decision-making about health means…
questions.memo: Responsible decisions weigh consequences and the facts before acting.

questions.question: HIV can be spread by sharing food or hugging.
questions.memo: HIV is not spread by everyday contact like sharing food, hugging or shaking hands.

questions.question: Knowing your status by getting ____ is a responsible health choice.
questions.memo: Getting tested means you know your status and can get treatment and prevent spread.

questions.question: Why is it important to have accurate information about HIV and AIDS?
options: It helps prevent infection and reduce stigma
questions.expected: It helps prevent infection and reduce stigma
questions.memo: Accurate information helps prevent infection and reduces harmful stigma.

questions.question: Supporting people living with HIV helps them stay healthy and hopeful.
questions.memo: Support helps people with HIV stick to treatment and stay healthy and hopeful.

questions.question: A safety issue linked to HIV care is to…
options: handle blood and wounds carefully and hygienically
questions.expected: handle blood and wounds carefully and hygienically
questions.memo: Careful, hygienic handling of blood and wounds is an important safety measure.

questions.question: Sort each statement into TRUE or FALSE about HIV and AIDS.

items.text: HIV can be managed with ARV treatment
People with HIV deserve respect and care
You can tell who has HIV by looking

questions.expected: ARV treatment and deserving respect are true; spreading by hugging or telling by looks are false.
questions.memo: Know the facts: HIV is manageable and not spread by everyday contact; stigma is based on myths.

questions.question: Put the steps of responsible action around HIV health in order.

items.text: Get tested to know your status
Get treatment and support if needed

questions.expected: Get accurate info, make safe choices, get tested, then get treatment and support if needed.
questions.memo: Responsible steps: be informed, choose safely, test, and access treatment and support.

questions.question: The key message about HIV and AIDS is that it should be met with…
questions.memo: HIV is best met with accurate facts, prevention, treatment and compassion.

questions.question: Knowing your HIV status through testing lets you get treatment and stay healthy.
questions.memo: Testing means you know your status and can access treatment early to stay healthy.

LO.G8.CR.A1.title: Nation building
LO.G8.CR.A1.description: Constitutional rights & responsibilities (CAPS G8 T4) — Constitutional rights and responsibilities: Nation building.
LO.G8.CR.A1.recovery_strategy: Nation building means working together across our differences to build one united country.

questions.question: What does 'nation building' mean?
options: Working together across differences to build one united country
questions.expected: Working together across differences to build one united country
questions.memo: Nation building means uniting people of different backgrounds to build one country.

questions.question: Nation building can happen at home, at school and in the community.
questions.memo: Nation building can be promoted in different contexts: home, school and community.

questions.question: Which action promotes nation building?
options: Respecting and including people of all cultures
questions.expected: Respecting and including people of all cultures
questions.memo: Respect, inclusion and cooperation across cultures promote nation building.

questions.question: Bringing people together as one despite differences builds national ____.
questions.memo: Nation building creates national unity from diversity.

questions.question: How did Nelson Mandela contribute to nation building?
questions.memo: Mandela promoted forgiveness, reconciliation and unity — key to nation building.

questions.question: Both women and men, as individuals and groups, can build the nation.
questions.memo: Nation building includes the contributions of women and men, individuals and groups.

questions.question: Which national symbol helps unite South Africans?
questions.memo: Shared symbols like the flag and anthem help build a sense of national unity.

questions.question: Healing past divisions and rebuilding trust is called ____.
questions.memo: Reconciliation heals past divisions and rebuilds trust between people.

questions.question: A school project where different cultures share their food and music promotes…
questions.memo: Sharing cultures builds understanding, unity and respect for diversity.

questions.question: Nation building requires everyone to give up their own culture.
questions.memo: Nation building unites people while still respecting and celebrating their different cultures.

questions.question: Why is nation building important for South Africa?
options: It heals past divisions and builds a peaceful society
questions.expected: It heals past divisions and builds a peaceful society
questions.memo: Nation building helps heal South Africa's past divisions and build peace.

questions.question: An ordinary citizen can build the nation by…
options: volunteering and treating all people with respect
questions.expected: volunteering and treating all people with respect
questions.memo: Everyday acts of respect and service contribute to nation building.

questions.question: Sport, like supporting a national team, can promote unity.
questions.memo: Shared national sporting moments can bring people together and promote unity.

questions.question: Many cultures living together in respect shows 'unity in ____'.
questions.memo: 'Unity in diversity' means being united while respecting many cultures.

questions.question: Which attitude best supports nation building?
options: Tolerance and willingness to work with others
questions.expected: Tolerance and willingness to work with others
questions.memo: Tolerance and cooperation are attitudes that support nation building.

questions.question: Learning about other cultures can reduce prejudice.
questions.memo: Understanding other cultures reduces prejudice and supports unity.

questions.question: Sort each action into PROMOTES nation building or HARMS it.
questions.expected: Celebrating heritage and respecting languages promote; racism and exclusion harm nation building.
questions.memo: Inclusion and respect build the nation; prejudice and exclusion break it down.

questions.question: Put the steps for a class nation-building project in order.

items.text: Decide on a unifying theme (e.g. our cultures)
Invite everyone to share their heritage
Hold the event with respect and inclusion
Reflect on what united the group

questions.expected: Choose a unifying theme, invite sharing, hold an inclusive event, then reflect on what united you.
questions.memo: Build unity by choosing a shared theme, inviting participation, including all, and reflecting.

questions.question: The core idea of nation building is…
options: many people, one united and respectful nation
questions.expected: many people, one united and respectful nation
questions.memo: Nation building unites diverse people into one respectful nation.

questions.question: Respecting all of South Africa's official languages supports nation building.
questions.memo: Valuing every official language helps people feel included and builds national unity.

LO.G8.CR.A2.title: Human rights violations
LO.G8.CR.A2.description: Constitutional rights & responsibilities (CAPS G8 T4) — Constitutional rights and responsibilities: Human rights violations.
LO.G8.CR.A2.recovery_strategy: A human rights violation is when someone's rights are denied; we counter it by speaking up and acting.

questions.question: What is a human rights VIOLATION?
options: When someone's rights are denied or taken away
questions.expected: When someone's rights are denied or taken away
questions.memo: A human rights violation happens when a person's rights are denied or taken away.

questions.question: Unfair discrimination is a type of human rights violation.
questions.memo: Unfair discrimination denies people equal rights and is a violation.

questions.question: Which is an example of a human rights violation?
options: Stopping a child from going to school
questions.expected: Stopping a child from going to school
questions.memo: Denying education violates a person's right to education.

questions.question: Treating people unfairly because of race or gender is unfair ____.
questions.memo: Unfair discrimination treats people unequally based on things like race or gender.

questions.question: Which is a COUNTER-STRATEGY to human rights violations?
options: Reporting and standing up against the violation
questions.expected: Reporting and standing up against the violation
questions.memo: Counter-strategies include reporting, speaking up and supporting victims.

questions.question: Slavery and forced labour are serious human rights violations.
questions.memo: Slavery and forced labour deny basic freedoms and are grave violations.

questions.question: Where can a violation of human rights be reported?
options: The police or the Human Rights Commission
questions.expected: The police or the Human Rights Commission
questions.memo: Violations can be reported to the police or the South African Human Rights Commission.

questions.question: Speaking up for someone whose rights are denied is called being an ____.
questions.memo: An advocate speaks and acts to defend others' rights.

questions.question: Doing nothing while someone's rights are violated helps the situation.
questions.memo: Staying silent allows violations to continue; speaking up and reporting help.

questions.question: A worker is denied pay because of their religion. This is…
options: a human rights violation that can be reported
questions.expected: a human rights violation that can be reported
questions.memo: Denying pay due to religion is unfair discrimination — a reportable violation.

questions.question: Why is it important to know about human rights violations?
options: So you can recognise, prevent and report them
questions.expected: So you can recognise, prevent and report them
questions.memo: Knowing about violations helps you recognise, prevent and report them.

questions.question: Bullying that targets someone's race or religion can be a rights violation.
questions.memo: Targeting someone's race or religion through bullying violates their dignity and rights.

questions.question: Organisations that protect rights help ____ victims of violations.
questions.memo: Rights organisations support and protect victims of violations.

questions.question: Which is a positive counter-strategy a school can use?
options: Teaching respect and having anti-bullying rules
questions.expected: Teaching respect and having anti-bullying rules
questions.memo: Education about respect and clear anti-bullying rules counter rights violations.

questions.question: Everyone has a role in protecting human rights, not just the government.
questions.memo: Protecting rights is everyone's responsibility, not only the government's.

questions.question: The best response if you witness a clear rights violation is to…
options: safely report it to a trusted authority
questions.expected: safely report it to a trusted authority
questions.memo: Reporting to a trusted authority is the responsible response to a violation.

questions.question: Sort each into a human RIGHTS VIOLATION or RESPECT for rights.

items.text: Denying someone a job because of race
Forcing a child to work instead of school

questions.expected: Race-based denial and child labour are violations; equal treatment and freedom of religion respect rights.
questions.memo: Violations deny rights; respect upholds equality, freedom and dignity.

questions.question: Put the steps for responding to a human rights violation in order.

items.text: Recognise that a right is being violated
Stay safe and gather the facts
Report it to a trusted authority

questions.expected: Recognise the violation, stay safe and gather facts, report it, then support the victim.
questions.memo: Respond by recognising, staying safe, reporting and supporting the victim.

questions.question: The key message about human rights violations is that they should be…
questions.memo: Violations should be recognised, opposed and reported to protect everyone's rights.

questions.question: Knowing your rights helps you recognise when they, or others' rights, are violated.
questions.memo: Understanding your rights lets you spot and respond to violations against yourself and others.

LO.G8.CR.A3.title: Gender equity
LO.G8.CR.A3.description: Constitutional rights & responsibilities (CAPS G8 T4) — Constitutional rights and responsibilities: Gender equity.
LO.G8.CR.A3.recovery_strategy: Gender equity means fair treatment of all genders; gender-based violence is a crime with help available.

questions.question: What does 'gender equity' mean?
options: Fair and equal treatment of all genders
questions.expected: Fair and equal treatment of all genders
questions.memo: Gender equity means fair, equal treatment and opportunities for all genders.

questions.question: Girls and boys should have equal opportunities in sport and education.
questions.memo: Gender equity means equal opportunities in education, sport and life.

questions.question: Which is an example of a gender-equity issue in sport?
options: Girls' teams getting far fewer resources than boys'
questions.expected: Girls' teams getting far fewer resources than boys'
questions.memo: Unequal resources between girls' and boys' sport is a gender-equity issue.

questions.question: Violence aimed at someone because of their gender is gender-based ____.
questions.memo: Gender-based violence (GBV) is violence directed at someone because of their gender.

questions.question: Gender-based violence and rape are…
questions.memo: GBV and rape are serious crimes; the law protects victims and punishes offenders.

questions.question: Gender-based violence can have emotional, health and social impacts on victims.
questions.memo: GBV harms victims emotionally, physically and socially.

questions.question: Which helps PREVENT violence against women and girls?
options: Respect, equality and enforcing the law
questions.expected: Respect, equality and enforcing the law
questions.memo: Prevention rests on respect, equality, education and enforcing laws like the Sexual Offences Act.

questions.question: Victims of gender-based violence can find safety and help at a ____.
questions.memo: Shelters, the police and helplines offer safety and help to victims of GBV.

questions.question: Gender stereotypes, like 'girls can't lead', support gender equity.
questions.memo: Harmful stereotypes work against gender equity by limiting people unfairly.

questions.question: A girl is told she 'can't' study engineering because she is a girl. This is…
options: an unfair gender stereotype she has every right to challenge
questions.expected: an unfair gender stereotype she has every right to challenge
questions.memo: Telling someone they can't pursue a field due to gender is an unfair stereotype.

questions.question: Where can a victim of gender-based violence find help?
options: The police, a clinic, or a GBV helpline
questions.expected: The police, a clinic, or a GBV helpline
questions.memo: Police, clinics and GBV helplines provide help and safety for victims.

questions.question: Boys and men can also be affected by gender-based violence.
questions.memo: While women and girls are most affected, boys and men can also experience GBV.

questions.question: South Africa has a law on sexual ____ to protect victims.
questions.memo: The Sexual Offences Act protects victims and sets out penalties for offenders.

questions.question: Which attitude best supports gender equity?
questions.memo: Treating all genders as equal is the foundation of gender equity.

questions.question: Reporting gender-based violence helps protect the victim and others.
questions.memo: Reporting GBV helps protect victims and can prevent further harm.

questions.question: How can schools promote gender equity?
options: Equal opportunities and zero tolerance for abuse
questions.expected: Equal opportunities and zero tolerance for abuse
questions.memo: Equal opportunities and zero tolerance for abuse promote gender equity at school.

questions.question: Sort each into PROMOTES gender equity or WORKS AGAINST it.

items.text: Girls and boys both leading projects

questions.expected: Equal pay and shared leadership promote equity; gender stereotypes and excusing GBV work against it.
questions.memo: Equity grows from equal treatment; stereotypes and excusing violence undermine it.

questions.question: Put the steps for safely helping a friend who reports gender-based violence in order.

items.text: Reassure them it is not their fault
Help them reach a trusted adult or helpline
Support them as they get help

questions.expected: Listen and believe, reassure it is not their fault, help them reach help, then support them.
questions.memo: Support a survivor by believing them, reassuring them, connecting them to help and staying supportive.

questions.question: The key message of gender equity is that…
options: everyone deserves equal respect, rights and safety
questions.expected: everyone deserves equal respect, rights and safety
questions.memo: Gender equity means equal respect, rights and safety for everyone.

questions.question: Gender-based violence is never the victim's fault.
questions.memo: Responsibility for gender-based violence always lies with the abuser, never the victim.

LO.G8.CR.A4.title: Cultural diversity in South Africa
LO.G8.CR.A4.description: Constitutional rights & responsibilities (CAPS G8 T4) — Constitutional rights and responsibilities: Cultural diversity in South Africa.
LO.G8.CR.A4.recovery_strategy: South Africa's many cultures enrich us; respecting difference builds unity in diversity.

questions.question: What does 'cultural diversity' mean?
options: Many different cultures living in one society
questions.expected: Many different cultures living in one society
questions.memo: Cultural diversity means many different cultures existing together in a society.

questions.question: South Africa is often called the 'Rainbow Nation' because of its diversity.
questions.memo: South Africa's many cultures earned it the nickname 'Rainbow Nation'.

questions.question: Which is part of a culture?
questions.memo: Culture includes language, traditions, beliefs, food, music and customs.

questions.question: Valuing cultures different from your own shows ____ for diversity.
questions.memo: Respecting cultures different from your own is key to living in a diverse society.

questions.question: How can cultural norms and values influence behaviour?
options: They shape what people see as acceptable and important
questions.expected: They shape what people see as acceptable and important
questions.memo: Cultural norms and values influence attitudes, choices and behaviour.

questions.question: Learning about other cultures can enrich your own understanding.
questions.memo: Understanding diverse cultures enriches society and individuals.

questions.question: 'Celebrate unity in diversity' means we should…
options: respect differences and enjoy what we share
force everyone to be the same
questions.expected: respect differences and enjoy what we share
questions.memo: Unity in diversity means respecting differences while celebrating common bonds.

questions.question: Practices passed down in a culture, like ceremonies, are ____.
questions.memo: Traditions are cultural practices passed down through generations.

questions.question: Respecting difference includes respecting culture, religion and gender.
questions.memo: Respect for difference covers culture, religion and gender.

questions.question: A classmate eats different food for cultural reasons. The respectful response is to…
options: be curious and respectful, not mocking
questions.expected: be curious and respectful, not mocking
questions.memo: Curiosity and respect, not mockery, honour cultural difference.

questions.question: Why is cultural diversity a strength for South Africa?
options: It brings varied ideas, talents and traditions together
questions.expected: It brings varied ideas, talents and traditions together
questions.memo: Diversity brings together varied ideas, talents and traditions, enriching society.

questions.question: Stereotyping a whole culture is fair if it is 'just a joke'.
questions.memo: Stereotyping a culture is disrespectful and harmful, even as a 'joke'.

questions.question: Treating people of all cultures as equal upholds the value of ____.
questions.memo: Equality means treating people of all cultures fairly and as equals.

questions.question: Which event celebrates South Africa's cultural diversity?
questions.memo: Heritage Day celebrates the diverse cultures and heritage of South Africa.

questions.question: Diverse cultural norms can relate to personal and community issues.
questions.memo: Cultural norms and values relate to many personal and community matters.

questions.question: How should you respond if a tradition differs from your own beliefs?
options: Respect it while still holding your own values
questions.expected: Respect it while still holding your own values
questions.memo: You can respect others' traditions while keeping your own values.

questions.question: Sort each response to cultural difference into RESPECTFUL or DISRESPECTFUL.

items.text: Learning a greeting in a friend's language

questions.expected: Learning a greeting and asking politely are respectful; mocking and stereotyping are disrespectful.
questions.memo: Curiosity and politeness respect culture; mockery and stereotypes disrespect it.

questions.question: Put the steps for building respect in a diverse class in order.

items.text: Learn about the cultures around you
Celebrate both differences and shared bonds

questions.expected: Learn about cultures, listen, treat everyone equally, then celebrate differences and shared bonds.
questions.memo: Respect grows from learning, listening, equal treatment and celebrating unity in diversity.

questions.question: The key message about cultural diversity is that it is…
options: a strength to be respected and celebrated
questions.expected: a strength to be respected and celebrated
questions.memo: Cultural diversity is a strength to respect and celebrate.

questions.question: Learning a few words in a classmate's home language is a sign of respect.
questions.memo: Making an effort with someone's language shows genuine respect for their culture.

LO.G8.CR.A5.title: Religions and social development
LO.G8.CR.A5.description: Constitutional rights & responsibilities (CAPS G8 T4) — Constitutional rights and responsibilities: Religions and social development.
LO.G8.CR.A5.recovery_strategy: Faith-based organisations help society through charity, care and community upliftment.

questions.question: What is 'social development'?
questions.memo: Social development means improving people's wellbeing and the life of communities.

questions.question: Religious organisations often help people in need in their communities.
questions.memo: Many religious organisations contribute to social development through charity and care.

questions.question: Which is a way religious organisations contribute to social development?
questions.memo: Religious groups run soup kitchens, shelters, clinics and schools that aid social development.

questions.question: Giving help to those in need, often through charity, is called ____.
questions.memo: Outreach is reaching out to help those in need, often through charity work.

questions.question: A faith-based group provides free meals to homeless people. This supports…
options: social development and care for the vulnerable
questions.expected: social development and care for the vulnerable
questions.memo: Providing meals to the homeless supports social development and care for the vulnerable.

questions.question: Helping others is a value found across many religions.
questions.memo: Caring for others and charity are values shared by many religions.

questions.question: Which service might a religious organisation provide?
questions.memo: Religious organisations may provide education, healthcare and disaster relief.

questions.question: Organisations that help society without aiming for profit are ____-profit.
questions.memo: Non-profit organisations work to help society rather than to make profit.

questions.question: Only the government can contribute to social development.
questions.memo: Religious groups, NGOs and individuals all contribute to social development, not just government.

questions.question: How can young people support religious or community social development?
options: Volunteer time and help with projects
questions.expected: Volunteer time and help with projects
questions.memo: Volunteering time and helping with projects supports social development.

questions.question: During a flood, a religious group shelters and feeds families. This is an example of…
questions.memo: Sheltering and feeding flood victims is disaster relief and social care.

questions.question: Caring for the poor and sick is a common contribution of religions.
questions.memo: Caring for the poor and sick is a frequent religious contribution to society.

questions.question: People who help others without being paid are ____.
questions.memo: Volunteers give their time freely to help others and their community.

questions.question: Why are the contributions of religious organisations valuable to society?
options: They support people that other services may miss
questions.expected: They support people that other services may miss
questions.memo: Religious organisations often reach and support people other services may miss.

questions.question: Different religions can work together to help a community.
questions.memo: People of different religions can cooperate to support their community.

questions.question: Building a clinic or school is an example of contributing to…
questions.memo: Building clinics and schools contributes to long-term social development.

questions.question: Sort each action into SUPPORTS social development or DOES NOT.
questions.expected: Clinics and feeding programmes support development; ignoring or excluding the needy does not.
questions.memo: Social development helps the vulnerable; neglect and exclusion do not.

questions.question: Put the steps for a youth community-service project in order.

items.text: Identify a need in the community
Carry out the project with others

questions.expected: Identify a need, plan a project, carry it out with others, then reflect on the impact.
questions.memo: Serve well by identifying a need, planning, acting together and reflecting.

questions.question: The key message is that religions and community groups can…
options: make a real, positive difference in society
questions.expected: make a real, positive difference in society
questions.memo: Religious and community organisations can make a real, positive difference to society.

questions.question: Young people can contribute to social development by volunteering their time.
questions.memo: Volunteering time and skills lets young people contribute to social development.

LO.G8.WW.A1.title: Learning styles
LO.G8.WW.A1.description: World of work (CAPS G8 T2) — World of work: Learning styles.
LO.G8.WW.A1.recovery_strategy: Knowing your learning style (seeing, hearing, doing, reading) helps you study more effectively.

questions.question: What is a 'learning style'?
options: The way a person learns best
questions.expected: The way a person learns best
questions.memo: A learning style is the way an individual learns and takes in information best.

questions.question: Visual, aural, kinesthetic and reading/writing are types of learning styles.
questions.memo: Common learning styles include visual, aural, kinesthetic, and reading/writing.

questions.question: A VISUAL learner learns best by…
questions.memo: Visual learners learn best through seeing — diagrams, charts and images.

questions.question: A learner who learns best by listening is an ____ learner.
questions.memo: Aural (auditory) learners learn best by listening — to explanations, discussions or recordings.

questions.question: A KINESTHETIC learner learns best by…
questions.memo: Kinesthetic learners learn best by doing — hands-on, practical activities.

questions.question: Knowing your learning style can help you study more effectively.
questions.memo: Knowing your learning style lets you choose study methods that work best for you.

questions.question: A READING/WRITING learner learns best by…
questions.memo: Reading/writing learners learn best through reading and writing text.

questions.question: Most people learn using a ____ of styles, not just one.
questions.memo: Many people use a mix of learning styles rather than only one.

questions.question: There is one 'best' learning style that is right for everyone.
questions.memo: No single style suits everyone; people differ and often blend styles.

questions.question: Sipho remembers things best when he draws diagrams. His style is likely…
questions.memo: Learning best from drawing diagrams points to a visual learning style.

questions.question: How can a kinesthetic learner study spelling effectively?
options: Write or trace the words while saying them
questions.expected: Write or trace the words while saying them
questions.memo: Kinesthetic learners benefit from movement, like writing or tracing while learning.

questions.question: Applying your own learning style means choosing study methods that suit you.
questions.memo: Applying your learning style means picking study methods that match how you learn best.

questions.question: A learner who likes group discussion may favour the ____ style.
questions.memo: Enjoying discussion suggests an aural (listening and speaking) preference.

questions.question: Why is it useful to use more than one learning style?
options: It reinforces learning in different ways
questions.expected: It reinforces learning in different ways
questions.memo: Using several styles reinforces learning through different channels.

questions.question: A visual learner might use colour-coded notes and mind maps.
questions.memo: Colour-coding and mind maps suit visual learners well.

questions.question: How can knowing learning styles help in the world of work?
options: It helps you learn new job skills efficiently
questions.expected: It helps you learn new job skills efficiently
questions.memo: Knowing how you learn helps you pick up new job skills efficiently.

questions.question: Match each learner to a fitting study method by ordering the methods for Learner 1→4.

items.text: (Aural) Listen to and discuss the material

questions.expected: Visual→diagrams, aural→listen/discuss, kinesthetic→hands-on, reading/writing→read and summarise.
questions.memo: Each learning style has study methods that suit it best.

questions.question: Sort each study method into VISUAL or KINESTHETIC.
questions.expected: Mind maps and charts are visual; building models and acting out are kinesthetic.
questions.memo: Visual methods use seeing; kinesthetic methods use doing and moving.

questions.question: The main benefit of knowing your learning style is that you can…
options: study and learn in the way that works best for you
questions.expected: study and learn in the way that works best for you
questions.memo: Knowing your learning style lets you learn in the way that works best for you.

questions.question: Most people learn best by combining several learning styles.
questions.memo: Combining styles reinforces learning and suits how most people actually learn.

LO.G8.WW.A2.title: Six career categories
LO.G8.WW.A2.description: World of work (CAPS G8 T2) — World of work: Six career categories.
LO.G8.WW.A2.recovery_strategy: Careers group into six types; matching your interests to a type helps you choose a direction.

questions.question: How many main career categories are studied in Grade 8 LO?
questions.memo: The six career categories are investigative, enterprising, realistic, artistic, conventional and social.

questions.question: The six career categories include 'investigative' and 'artistic'.
questions.memo: The six categories are investigative, enterprising, realistic, artistic, conventional and social.

questions.question: Someone who loves solving puzzles and research suits which category?
questions.memo: Investigative careers suit people who enjoy research, analysis and solving problems.

questions.question: A person who loves art, music or design fits the ____ category.
questions.memo: Artistic careers suit creative people who enjoy art, music, writing or design.

questions.question: A 'realistic' career type usually involves…
questions.memo: Realistic careers involve practical, hands-on or outdoor work, like building or farming.

questions.question: A 'social' career type involves helping and working with people.
questions.memo: Social careers involve helping, teaching or caring for people.

questions.question: An 'enterprising' person is likely to enjoy…
questions.memo: Enterprising careers suit people who like leading, persuading and business.

questions.question: A 'conventional' person enjoys organised work with data and ____.
questions.memo: Conventional careers suit people who like organised, detailed work with data and records.

questions.question: Knowing your career category can guide your subject choices.
questions.memo: Matching your category to careers helps guide subject and study choices.

questions.question: Naledi loves caring for people and is patient. A fitting category is…
questions.memo: Patience and caring for people fit the social career category.

questions.question: How does work meet South Africa's social and economic needs?
options: It provides services, goods and jobs people need
questions.expected: It provides services, goods and jobs people need
questions.memo: Work provides services, goods and jobs that meet social and economic needs.

questions.question: Identifying needs in your community can reveal useful career paths.
questions.memo: Community needs point to careers that can meet those needs.

questions.question: Different categories need different thinking and ____ skills.
questions.memo: Each career category requires particular thinking and learning skills.

questions.question: Which school subjects suit an investigative (science) career?
questions.memo: Investigative science careers usually need sciences and mathematics.

questions.question: A person can have interests that fit more than one career category.
questions.memo: Many people's interests span more than one category.

questions.question: Why match your interests and abilities to a career category?
options: You are more likely to enjoy and do well at the work
questions.expected: You are more likely to enjoy and do well at the work
questions.memo: Matching interests and abilities to a category leads to more enjoyable, successful work.

questions.question: Match each career to its category by ordering the categories for Career 1→4.
questions.memo: Careers fall into categories based on the kind of work and interests they involve.

questions.question: Sort each career into the SOCIAL or REALISTIC category.
questions.expected: Teacher and counsellor are social; plumber and mechanic are realistic.
questions.memo: Social careers help people; realistic careers are practical and hands-on.

questions.question: The main use of the six career categories is to…
options: help you explore careers that match your interests
questions.expected: help you explore careers that match your interests
questions.memo: The categories help you explore careers matching your interests and abilities.

questions.question: A person's interests can fit more than one career category.
questions.memo: Many people have interests spanning several career categories, which widens their options.

LO.G8.WW.A3.title: School subjects and decision-making
LO.G8.WW.A3.description: World of work (CAPS G8 T2) — World of work: School subjects and decision-making.
LO.G8.WW.A3.recovery_strategy: Your strengths in subjects hint at careers; good decisions weigh interest, ability and passion.

questions.question: How can your performance in school subjects help with career choices?
options: Strong subjects can point to suitable careers
Subjects have no link to careers
questions.expected: Strong subjects can point to suitable careers
questions.memo: Your strengths in subjects hint at careers that may suit your abilities.

questions.question: Your interests and abilities are both worth considering for a career.
questions.memo: Good career decisions weigh both interests and abilities.

questions.question: Which is a THEORETICAL type of learning activity?
questions.memo: Theoretical activities involve ideas, reading and discussion rather than hands-on work.

questions.question: Doing experiments and building models are ____ activities.
questions.memo: Practical activities are hands-on, like experiments and building models.

questions.question: Why think about the 'demands' of a subject?
options: Different subjects need different thinking and skills
questions.expected: Different subjects need different thinking and skills
questions.memo: Each subject demands particular thinking and learning skills.

questions.question: Good decision-making considers your strengths, interests and goals.
questions.memo: Sound decisions weigh your strengths, interests, abilities and goals.

questions.question: What is the FIRST step in a good decision-making process?
options: Understand the decision and gather information
questions.expected: Understand the decision and gather information
questions.memo: Good decisions start with understanding the choice and gathering information.

questions.question: A subject you both enjoy and do well in matches your interest and ____.
questions.memo: A subject you enjoy and do well in matches both interest and ability.

questions.question: Choosing a career direction should ignore what you are good at.
questions.memo: Your abilities matter; ignoring them leads to poor career decisions.

questions.question: Sipho loves Mathematics and solving problems but dislikes art. A sensible direction is…
questions.memo: Matching his maths strength and problem-solving interest points to a maths/science field.

questions.question: Which is a GROUP learning activity?
questions.memo: Group activities, like team projects, involve working with others.

questions.question: Knowing how you like to learn can help you choose suitable subjects.
questions.memo: Understanding your learning preferences helps with subject and career choices.

questions.question: Choosing a career that fits your strength, ability, interest and ____ leads to satisfaction.
questions.memo: Decisions linking strength, ability, interest and passion lead to satisfying careers.

questions.question: Why gather information before making a career-related decision?
options: To make an informed choice, not a guess
questions.expected: To make an informed choice, not a guess
questions.memo: Gathering information leads to informed decisions rather than guesses.

questions.question: It is wise to consider several options before deciding on a direction.
questions.memo: Weighing several options leads to better decisions than choosing the first idea.

questions.question: A balanced decision considers…
options: interests, abilities, demands and goals together
questions.expected: interests, abilities, demands and goals together
questions.memo: Balanced decisions weigh interests, abilities, subject demands and goals.

questions.question: Put the steps of a good decision-making process in order.

items.text: Understand the decision to be made
Weigh the options against your strengths and goals
Make the choice and review it later

questions.expected: Understand the decision, gather options, weigh them against strengths and goals, then choose and review.
questions.memo: Decide well by understanding, gathering options, weighing them, and choosing then reviewing.

questions.question: Sort each learning activity into THEORETICAL or PRACTICAL.
questions.expected: Discussing and reading are theoretical; experiments and wiring are practical.
questions.memo: Theoretical work uses ideas and text; practical work is hands-on.

questions.question: The key idea linking school subjects and careers is to…
options: use your strengths and interests to guide informed choices
questions.expected: use your strengths and interests to guide informed choices
questions.memo: Use your subject strengths and interests to make informed career decisions.

questions.question: Considering several options leads to better decisions than choosing the first idea.

LO.G9.DS.A1.caps_topic: Development of the self in society

questions.question: What is goal-setting?

questions.question: A personal lifestyle choice is a decision about how you live, like diet or activity.

questions.question: Which can INFLUENCE personal lifestyle choices?
options: Media, family, friends, culture and community

questions.question: Making a decision based on facts and thought is an ____ decision.

questions.question: What does being ASSERTIVE help you do with lifestyle choices?

questions.question: A SMART goal is specific, measurable, achievable, relevant and time-bound.

questions.question: Which is a POSITIVE influence on lifestyle choices?
options: A friend who encourages exercise and study

questions.question: A goal you want to reach soon is a ____-term goal.

questions.question: Outside influences should always decide your lifestyle for you.

questions.question: Naledi's friends pressure her to skip training. Using assertiveness, she should…
options: calmly stick to her goal and say no

questions.question: Why set goals for your lifestyle?
options: They limit you for no reason

questions.question: Reviewing and adjusting your goals over time is a good habit.
questions.memo: Reviewing and adjusting goals keeps them realistic and relevant.

questions.question: Recognising both positive and negative ____ helps you choose wisely.
questions.memo: Knowing positive and negative influences helps you make wise lifestyle choices.

questions.question: A negative influence on lifestyle choices could be…
options: pressure to use substances or skip school
questions.expected: pressure to use substances or skip school
questions.memo: Negative influences push unhealthy or risky choices.

questions.question: Confident, firm decision-making is part of assertiveness.
questions.memo: Assertiveness includes making confident, firm decisions.

questions.question: Which is the best response to an influence you disagree with?
options: Weigh it, then make your own informed choice
questions.expected: Weigh it, then make your own informed choice
questions.memo: Weighing influences and choosing for yourself leads to good decisions.

questions.question: A realistic short-term goal for a learner could be…
options: improving a subject mark by next term
questions.expected: improving a subject mark by next term
questions.memo: Realistic short-term goals are specific and achievable, like improving a mark by next term.

questions.question: Sort each influence on lifestyle choices into POSITIVE or NEGATIVE.

items.text: Friends daring you to break the law

questions.expected: Mentors and supportive family are positive; pressure to use drugs or break the law is negative.
questions.memo: Positive influences encourage healthy goals; negative ones push risky behaviour.

questions.question: Put the steps of setting and reaching a personal goal in order.

items.text: Decide on a clear, realistic goal
Make a plan with smaller steps
Take action and track your progress
Review and adjust the goal as needed

questions.expected: Decide on a clear goal, plan smaller steps, act and track progress, then review and adjust.
questions.memo: Reach goals by deciding, planning, acting and reviewing.

questions.question: The key idea of goal-setting and lifestyle choices is to…
options: make your own informed, assertive choices about how you live
questions.expected: make your own informed, assertive choices about how you live
questions.memo: Goal-setting and lifestyle choices are about making your own informed, assertive decisions.

LO.G9.DS.A2.title: Sexual behaviour and sexual health
LO.G9.DS.A2.description: Development of the self in society (CAPS G9 T1) — Development of the self in society: Sexual behaviour and sexual health.
LO.G9.DS.A2.strand: Development of the self in society · Term 1
LO.G9.DS.A2.caps_topic: Development of the self in society
LO.G9.DS.A2.recovery_strategy: Healthy choices like abstinence protect you from STIs, HIV and teenage pregnancy.

questions.question: What is a RISK FACTOR for unhealthy sexual behaviour?
questions.memo: Risk factors include peer pressure, substance use and lack of information.

questions.question: Abstinence is the most effective way to avoid pregnancy and STIs.
questions.memo: Abstinence is the most effective way to prevent pregnancy and sexually transmitted infections.

questions.question: Which is a possible result of unhealthy sexual behaviour?
questions.memo: Unhealthy sexual behaviour can lead to teenage pregnancy, STIs, HIV and emotional harm.

questions.question: Infections passed through sexual contact are called ____.
questions.memo: Sexually transmitted infections (STIs) are passed through sexual contact.

questions.question: Which factor can influence personal sexual behaviour?
options: Family, friends, peers and community norms
questions.expected: Family, friends, peers and community norms
questions.memo: Family, friends, peers and community norms all influence personal behaviour.

questions.question: Teenage pregnancy can have serious consequences for the teen parents and the child.
questions.memo: Teenage pregnancy can have adverse consequences for the teen parents and their children.

questions.question: A strategy to deal with unhealthy sexual behaviour is…
questions.memo: Strategies include abstinence and changing risky behaviour, plus getting support.

questions.question: Things that lower your risk, like good support, are ____ factors.
questions.memo: Protective factors, like support and information, lower the risk of harmful behaviour.

questions.question: It is unwise to seek accurate information about sexual health.
questions.memo: Seeking accurate information helps you make safe, healthy decisions.

questions.question: Where can a teenager find support and protection against risky behaviour?
options: A clinic, counsellor or trusted community structure
questions.expected: A clinic, counsellor or trusted community structure
questions.memo: Clinics, counsellors and community structures offer support and protection.

questions.question: Sipho feels pressured into risky behaviour 'to prove himself.' The healthiest response is to…
options: stay firm on his values and seek support if needed
questions.expected: stay firm on his values and seek support if needed
questions.memo: Standing firm on values and seeking support is the healthiest, safest response.

questions.question: Substance use can increase the chance of risky sexual behaviour.
questions.memo: Substance use lowers judgement and can increase risky sexual behaviour.

questions.question: Choosing not to have sex is called ____.
questions.memo: Abstinence means choosing not to have sex, the most effective protection.

questions.question: Why is it important to know the consequences of risky behaviour?
options: So you can make informed, protective choices
It is none of your business
questions.expected: So you can make informed, protective choices
questions.memo: Knowing consequences helps you make informed, protective choices.

questions.question: Low self-image can be both a cause and a result of unhealthy sexual behaviour.
questions.memo: Low self-image can lead to and result from unhealthy sexual behaviour.

questions.question: Caring community structures can offer young people…
options: protection and resilience against high-risk behaviour
questions.expected: protection and resilience against high-risk behaviour
questions.memo: Supportive community structures build resilience against high-risk behaviour.

questions.question: Which is the most reliable source of sexual-health information?
options: A clinic nurse or health professional
questions.expected: A clinic nurse or health professional
questions.memo: Health professionals give the most reliable sexual-health information.

questions.question: Sort each factor into RISK or PROTECTIVE for sexual health.
questions.expected: Substance use and peer pressure are risks; accurate info and strong values are protective.
questions.memo: Risk factors raise the chance of harm; protective factors lower it.

questions.question: Put the steps for making a safe, healthy decision under pressure in order.

items.text: Know your own values and goals
Recognise the risk in the situation
Seek support if you need it

questions.expected: Know your values, recognise the risk, make a firm informed choice, then seek support if needed.
questions.memo: Decide safely by knowing your values, spotting risk, choosing firmly and seeking support.

questions.question: The key message about sexual health is to make…
options: informed, value-based choices that protect your health and future
questions.expected: informed, value-based choices that protect your health and future
questions.memo: Sexual health is protected by informed, value-based choices.

LO.G9.DS.A3.title: Challenging situations
LO.G9.DS.A3.description: Development of the self in society (CAPS G9 T1) — Development of the self in society: Challenging situations.
LO.G9.DS.A3.strand: Development of the self in society · Term 1
LO.G9.DS.A3.caps_topic: Development of the self in society
LO.G9.DS.A3.recovery_strategy: Tough emotions are normal; healthy coping and asking for help work better than alcohol or drugs.

questions.question: Which is an example of a CHALLENGING emotional situation?
options: Grief after losing a loved one
questions.expected: Grief after losing a loved one
questions.memo: Challenging situations include depression, grief, loss, trauma and crisis.

questions.question: Depression is more than ordinary sadness and can need support to manage.
questions.memo: Depression is a serious low mood, more than ordinary sadness, that often needs support.

questions.question: What is 'grief'?
options: Deep sadness, usually after a loss
questions.expected: Deep sadness, usually after a loss
questions.memo: Grief is the deep sadness people feel after a loss, such as a death.

questions.question: A sudden, very difficult event that overwhelms a person is a ____.
questions.memo: A crisis is a sudden, overwhelming event that is hard to cope with.

questions.question: Which is a HEALTHY way to cope with strong emotions?
questions.memo: Healthy coping includes talking to trusted people, not using substances or harming others.

questions.question: Using alcohol or drugs to cope is a counterproductive coping technique.
questions.memo: Using alcohol or drugs is counterproductive — it worsens problems rather than solving them.

questions.question: What can CAUSE trauma?
questions.memo: Trauma can result from frightening or harmful experiences like accidents or abuse.

questions.question: Reaching out to a counsellor or trusted adult is asking for ____.
questions.memo: Asking a counsellor or trusted adult for help is a healthy response to difficult emotions.

questions.question: Asking for help when you are struggling is a sign of strength.
questions.memo: Reaching out for help takes courage and is a sign of strength, not weakness.

questions.question: A friend seems very low for weeks and talks about hopelessness. You should…
options: encourage them to get help and tell a trusted adult
tell them to 'snap out of it'
questions.expected: encourage them to get help and tell a trusted adult
questions.memo: Persistent hopelessness needs support; encourage help and involve a trusted adult.

questions.question: Which is a problem-solving step for dealing with a tough emotion?
options: Name the feeling and think of healthy responses
questions.expected: Name the feeling and think of healthy responses
questions.memo: Problem-solving means naming the feeling and choosing healthy responses.

questions.question: Everyone faces difficult emotions at some point; they are part of life.
questions.memo: Difficult emotions are a normal part of life that everyone faces sometimes.

questions.question: Ongoing low mood and loss of interest can be signs of ____.
questions.memo: Ongoing low mood and loss of interest can be signs of depression.

questions.question: Where can a teenager get help for serious emotional difficulties?
options: A counsellor, clinic or helpline like SADAG
questions.expected: A counsellor, clinic or helpline like SADAG
questions.memo: Counsellors, clinics and helplines like SADAG offer help for emotional difficulties.

questions.question: Talking about feelings can help reduce their power over you.
questions.memo: Expressing feelings to someone you trust can ease their intensity.

questions.question: Which healthy strategy can help manage stress and strong emotions?
options: Exercise, rest, and talking to someone
questions.expected: Exercise, rest, and talking to someone
questions.memo: Exercise, rest and talking are healthy strategies to manage stress and emotions.

questions.question: Sort each coping response into HEALTHY or COUNTERPRODUCTIVE.
questions.expected: Counselling and exercise are healthy; using alcohol or bottling up are counterproductive.
questions.memo: Healthy coping faces feelings with support; counterproductive coping avoids or numbs them.

questions.question: Put the steps for responding to a difficult emotion in order.

items.text: Choose a healthy way to respond
Get professional help if it continues

questions.expected: Notice and name the emotion, choose a healthy response, talk to someone, then get help if it continues.
questions.memo: Handle hard emotions by naming them, responding healthily, talking, and getting help if needed.

questions.question: It is okay to need time to recover from grief or loss.
questions.memo: Recovering from grief or loss takes time, and that is normal and healthy.

questions.question: The key message about challenging situations is that…
options: healthy coping and seeking help are signs of strength
questions.expected: healthy coping and seeking help are signs of strength
questions.memo: Healthy coping and asking for help are signs of strength, not weakness.

LO.G9.HE.A1.title: Volunteerism
LO.G9.HE.A1.description: Health, social & environmental responsibility (CAPS G9 T3) — Health, social and environmental responsibility: Volunteerism.
LO.G9.HE.A1.recovery_strategy: Volunteering is giving your time to help others and your community without being paid.

questions.question: What is volunteerism?
options: Giving your time to help others without being paid
questions.expected: Giving your time to help others without being paid
questions.memo: Volunteerism is freely giving your time and effort to help others and the community.

questions.question: Volunteers usually work without being paid.
questions.memo: Volunteers give their time freely, usually without payment.

questions.question: Which is an example of volunteering?
options: Being paid for a full-time job

questions.question: Organisations that help society without making profit are ____ organisations.
questions.memo: Non-profit and community-based organisations help society rather than make profit.

questions.question: How does volunteering benefit the COMMUNITY?
options: It meets needs and improves social and environmental health
questions.expected: It meets needs and improves social and environmental health
questions.memo: Volunteering meets community needs and improves social and environmental health.

questions.question: Volunteering can also benefit the volunteer, building skills and confidence.
questions.memo: Volunteers gain skills, experience, confidence and a sense of purpose.

questions.question: Which is a 'community-based organisation'?
options: A local group helping its own community
questions.expected: A local group helping its own community
questions.memo: Community-based organisations are local groups that serve their own communities.

questions.question: Helping people who are less ____ is a common volunteer activity.
questions.memo: Volunteers often help those who are less privileged or in need.

questions.question: Volunteering is both an individual and a community responsibility.
questions.memo: Caring for others is both a personal and a shared community responsibility.

questions.question: A group helping people affected by HIV and AIDS is doing volunteer work that…
options: supports health and dignity in the community
questions.expected: supports health and dignity in the community
questions.memo: Helping those affected by HIV and AIDS supports community health and dignity.

questions.question: Why might a young person choose to volunteer?
options: To help others, gain skills and make a difference

questions.memo: Young people volunteer to help others, build skills and make a positive difference.

questions.question: Volunteer work can support sustainable development.
questions.memo: Volunteering can contribute to social, environmental and sustainable development.

questions.question: Caring for the environment, like a clean-up, is ____ volunteering.
questions.memo: Environmental volunteering includes activities like clean-ups and tree planting.

questions.question: Which is a type of volunteer activity?
questions.memo: Free tutoring, caring for the sick, and clean-ups are all volunteer activities.

questions.question: Even small acts of volunteering can make a real difference.
questions.memo: Small, consistent volunteer efforts add up to real community benefit.

options: help with a short local project on weekends
promise huge commitments she can't keep
wait until she is an adult
questions.expected: help with a short local project on weekends
questions.memo: Realistic, manageable volunteering fits her time while still making a difference.

questions.question: Sort each activity into VOLUNTEER work or PAID/NON-volunteer work.
questions.expected: Free park clean-ups and unpaid shelter help are volunteering; paid jobs and profit businesses are not.
questions.memo: Volunteering is unpaid help for others; paid work is done for income.

questions.question: Put the steps for starting a volunteer project in order.

items.text: Identify a need you care about
Find or form a group to help
Plan and carry out the activity

questions.expected: Identify a need, find a group, plan and act, then reflect on the difference made.
questions.memo: Volunteer well by identifying a need, gathering helpers, acting and reflecting.

questions.question: Volunteering can build skills that are useful in future work.
questions.memo: Volunteering builds skills, experience and confidence useful in future work.

questions.question: The key message about volunteerism is that it…
options: benefits both the community and the volunteer
questions.expected: benefits both the community and the volunteer
questions.memo: Volunteering benefits the community and the volunteer alike.

LO.G9.HE.A2.title: Violence and safety
LO.G9.HE.A2.description: Health, social & environmental responsibility (CAPS G9 T3) — Health, social and environmental responsibility: Violence and safety.
LO.G9.HE.A2.recovery_strategy: Violence harms everyone; conflict can be solved with communication and problem-solving instead.

questions.question: Which is a common act of violence that can happen in communities?
questions.memo: Common acts of violence include assault, robbery, bullying and abuse.

questions.question: Violence can occur at home, at school and in the community.
questions.memo: Violence can happen in many places — home, school and the wider community.

questions.question: Which can be a REASON violence occurs in communities?
options: Poverty, substance abuse and unresolved conflict
